newsitem.title: USA: Blood bank exec sees possible summer blood drought.
newsitem.headline: Blood bank exec sees possible summer blood drought.

text.p: America's blood supply could have one of its worst shortages in years this summer due to corporate downsizing and a lack of donations from baby boomers and "generation X-ers," a blood bank executive said Wednesday.

"We're not declaring a national blood shortage," Jim MacPherson, executive director of the non-profit America's Blood Centers, said. "We're trying to prepare you for the fact that this summer may be one of the worst that we have seen in many years."

Summer is customarily a time when blood donations drop, but this season could see deeper shortages because of societal changes, MacPherson said, citing corporate downsizing as the primary reason for current shortages.

"We're ... seeing increased resistence from corporate America to blood donation. Blood donation costs them money and they've figured it out. It costs them money because it's a loss of productivity and they have to give the employees time off to do it," he said.

Corporations are not ruling out blood drives but are willing to do fewer of them, according to MacPherson, whose organization represents blood donation centers that provide about 45 percent of the U.S. blood supply. The Red Cross provides approximately 45 percent and the rest is provided by hospitals, MacPherson said.

A generational shift has also cut into the stream of donated blood, he said. "The World War II generation, the very loyal people who used to donate habitually every eight weeks ... they're retiring, they're becoming too old to donate, they're dying off," he said at a briefing.
"And the baby boomers and the Gen-X does not have the same devotion to ... the culture of donation that we saw in the previous generation."

In addition, blood banks in ABC's network defer donation by people with various risk factors -- notably for AIDS and hepatitis -- and as more risk factors are identified this cuts into the amount of available blood for transfusions.

Even as supply declines, demand has been increasing in recent years, largely because of more sophisticated procedures including for cancer treatments and bone marrow transplants, which use a lot of blood, MacPherson said.

Some of these procedures, which are generally considered to be elective rather than emergency surgeries, can be delayed briefly, but the nightmare scenario for a summer blood shortage remains a traumatic accident with high casualties.
"The worst scenario for this summer is the bus that gets hit by the tractor-trailer and the blood isn't on the shelves to take care of the people," MacPherson said.
